claim: Consolidated billing combines usage across all accounts in the organization, which shares volume pricing discounts, Reserved Instance discounts and Savings Plans, and it is offered at no additional cost.
question: How does consolidated billing lower the bill, and what does it cost?

values.display: combine the usage across all accounts in the organization
shares the volume pricing discounts, Reserved Instance discounts
offered at no additional cost

evidence.quote: You can combine the usage across all accounts in the organization. This shares the volume pricing discounts, Reserved Instance discounts, and Savings Plans.
Consolidated billing is offered at no additional cost.

claim: For billing, AWS treats all accounts in the organization as one account and combines their usage to decide which volume pricing tiers apply.
question: How does consolidated billing apply volume pricing tiers?

values.display: as if they were one account
AWS combines the usage from all accounts

qualifiers.scope: services with volume pricing tiers, for example data transfer and Amazon S3

evidence.quote: For billing purposes, AWS treats all of the accounts in the organization as if they were one account.
With consolidated billing, AWS combines the usage from all accounts to determine which volume pricing tiers to apply, giving you a lower overall price whenever possible.

claim: Each month AWS charges the management account owner, not the member account owners; member accounts can still see their own usage and charges but not those of other accounts.
question: Who is charged each month in an organization, and what can member accounts see?

values.display: AWS charges the management account owner
they can still see their usage and charges
They can't view or obtain data

evidence.quote: Each month, AWS charges the management account owner, and not the owners of the member accounts.

Although the owners of the member accounts aren't charged, they can still see their usage and charges by going to their AWS Bills pages. They can't view or obtain data for the management account or any other member accounts on the bill.

claim: In an organization, AWS applies the free tier to the total usage across all accounts, not to each account individually.
question: Does each account in an organization get its own free tier?

values.display: applies the free tier to the total usage across all accounts
doesn't apply the free tier to each account individually

qualifiers.scope: services that support a free tier, in an organization

evidence.quote: For services such as Amazon EC2 that support a free tier, AWS applies the free tier to the total usage across all accounts in an AWS organization. AWS doesn't apply the free tier to each account individually.

Activate or deactivate sharing for individual accounts

Account-level control: Activate or deactivate sharing for individual accounts

evidence.heading: Sharing Modes

evidence.quote: After satisfying the account owner, remaining benefits can be shared with other organization accounts
evidence.heading: Sharing Modes

cost allocation tags manager

evidence.quote: Only the management account in an organization and single accounts that aren't members of an organization have access to the cost allocation tags manager in the Billing console.

claim: An organization trail created in the management account logs events for all accounts, applies to all member accounts automatically, and member accounts can see it but cannot modify or delete it; by default they cannot read its log files in S3.
question: Can users in a member account change or delete an organization trail?

values.display: Member accounts can see the organization trail
can't modify or delete it
member accounts don't have access to the log files

evidence.quote: Using AWS CloudTrail, a user in a management account can create an organization trail that logs all events for all AWS accounts in that organization. Organization trails are automatically applied to all member accounts in the organization. Member accounts can see the organization trail, but can't modify or delete it. By default, member accounts don't have access to the log files for the organization trail in the Amazon S3 bucket.

claim: You must sign in with the management account to create an organization trail.

to create an organization trail

claim: To protect member accounts from accidental closure, attach an IAM policy that denies account closure, listing protected accounts by ARN or matching them by tag with aws:ResourceTag.
question: How can an organization protect member accounts from being closed?

values.display: create an IAM policy that specifies which accounts are exempt
Tag individual accounts and use the aws:ResourceTag

evidence.quote: To protect member accounts from accidental closure, create an IAM policy that specifies which accounts are exempt. This policy prevents closure of protected member accounts.
Tag individual accounts and use the aws:ResourceTag global condition key to prevent closure of tagged accounts.

claim: OUs group accounts to administer them as one unit: a policy-based control attached to an OU is inherited automatically by all accounts in the OU, and accounts can move from one OU to another.
question: Why attach policies to OUs instead of to single accounts?

values.display: to administer as a single unit
all accounts within the OU automatically inherit the policy
you can move accounts from one OU to another

evidence.quote: You can use organizational units (OUs) to group accounts together to administer as a single unit.
For example, you can attach a policy-based control to an OU, and all accounts within the OU automatically inherit the policy.
Each OU can contain multiple accounts, and you can move accounts from one OU to another.

claim: AWS recommends one organization for all your accounts, because an organization is a security boundary that keeps policies and configuration consistent across accounts.
question: Should a company use one organization or several?

values.display: creating a single organization
An organization is a security boundary

evidence.quote: We recommend creating a single organization and managing all your accounts within this organization. An organization is a security boundary that lets you maintain consistency across accounts in your environment.

claim: AWS recommends isolating production workloads under top-level workload OUs and basing OUs on a common set of controls, not on the company's reporting structure, with separate non-production OUs for development and test.
question: How should OUs be designed according to AWS?

values.display: based on a common set of controls
rather than mirroring your company’s reporting structure

evidence.quote: We recommend that you isolate production workload environments and data under your top-level workload-oriented OUs. Your OUs should be based on a common set of controls rather than mirroring your company’s reporting structure.

claim: An AWS account gives natural security, access and billing boundaries, and multiple accounts let you distribute account-level quotas and API request-rate limits; production should be in separate accounts from test and development.
question: Why separate workloads into multiple accounts?

distribute account level quotas and API request-rate limits
separate production workloads from test/development workloads

evidence.quote: There are benefits of using multiple accounts because it lets you distribute account level quotas and API request-rate limits, and additional benefits listed here.
An AWS account provides natural security, access, and billing boundaries for your AWS resources.

claim: After root access management is enabled, newly created member accounts have no root user credentials, and accounts created in Organizations have no root user credentials by default.
question: Do new member accounts have root user credentials?

values.display: newly created member accounts are secure-by-default
have no root user credentials by default

qualifiers.scope: member accounts created in AWS Organizations

evidence.quote: After root access management is enabled, newly created member accounts are secure-by-default, having no root user credentials, which eliminates the need for additional security, such as MFA after provisioning.
New accounts you create in Organizations have no root user credentials by default.

claim: Trusted access lets a supported AWS service perform tasks in your organization and its accounts on your behalf by creating service-linked roles; it does not otherwise change the permissions of users or roles.
question: What is trusted access for an integrated service?

values.display: perform tasks in your organization and its accounts on your behalf
create an IAM role called a service-linked role

evidence.quote: You can use trusted access to enable a supported AWS service that you specify, called the trusted service, to perform tasks in your organization and its accounts on your behalf. This involves granting permissions to the trusted service but does not otherwise affect the permissions for users or roles. When you enable access, the trusted service can create an IAM role called a service-linked role in every account in your organization whenever that role is needed.

claim: Disabling trusted access does not stop users and roles with the right permissions from using the service; to block them, remove their IAM permissions or use SCPs, which apply only to member accounts.
question: Does disabling trusted access block users from using that service?

values.display: does not prevent users and roles
You can apply SCPs to only member accounts

qualifiers.scope: trusted access for an integrated service

evidence.quote: Disabling trusted service access does not prevent users and roles with appropriate permissions from using that service. To completely block users and roles from accessing an AWS service, you can remove the IAM permissions that grant that access, or you can use service control policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations.
You can apply SCPs to only member accounts. SCPs don't apply to the management account.
